statements: Vincent gains time-travel powers at age nineteen in 2025 and operates in the past as Adam Pleskot.
His foreknowledge remains secret.
Adam used knowledge of the original timeline to identify investment opportunities and anticipate emerging demand.
As his companies changed markets, he combined that knowledge with contemporary research, customer evidence and production planning.
His public explanation was disciplined data analysis; the origin of his advantage remained secret.
Throughout the story, Adam uses his foresight to anticipate demand and always maintains supply capacity at forecast demand plus 5%, keeping that reserve available to respond to demand.
This is good-output supply headroom, not an increase in forecast sales or a requirement to hold permanent excess stock.
Equipment utilisation and protection against a failed production tool are planned separately.
Inventory for anticipated demand peaks is funded a quarter in advance.
Wafer supply, tool redundancy and supplier lead times are planned and funded as separate protections.
Compete with IBM, present products at NCC from 1978 and COMDEX from 1979 onward, and manufacture at the maximum feasible scale to achieve standard-setting market coverage.
Develop customer trust and a loyal network of users, software developers and peripheral manufacturers through integrated hardware, software, training and support.
Adam established a secret engineering facility outside Logix Tech, AION Labs and AION Software.

He equipped it with a CAD workstation running Virtuoso, Spectre, Xcelium, Genus, Innovus, Tempus, Quantus and Pegasus, together with a HEIDELBERG DWL 66+ laser-lithography system brought from the 2020s.
The facility supplied advanced design work to the companies while concealing the origin of its tools.

From February 1975, Adam can supply circuit designs, design-rule checks, test structures, mask data and master masks to accelerate memory development. Cambridge must verify mask tone, scale, overlay, defects and compatibility with its projection tools and qualify its own silicon.

The secret facility supplies no commercial wafer capacity, automatic licence rights or transferred production qualification. Contemporary process-transfer and second-source rights require separate agreements.
Gordon Letwin never joins Microsoft; Tim Paterson never develops QDOS or becomes available to Microsoft in this timeline.
Hire staff, establish software-development environments, computer manufacturing and R&D, and a conservative semiconductor operation.

Logix alone develops the Apple II and S-100 expansion cards; these demonstrate Adam’s ecosystem intentions and are not DRI obligations.
Apple cards expose FlexiBUS and video to native Apple software.
CP/M-6502 is deferred, with no product, schedule or cost commitment.
Published interfaces and affordable developer access permit competing software, cards, peripherals and monitors.
AION retains Abacus, C tools, Business Tools, AIONix and the existing Pulse offering; DRI licenses CP/M independently.
SSG operates independently under its own brand from the cooperation period.

SSG owns General Ledger and its adaptations throughout; AION sponsors defined porting and networking work without equity, application ownership or a share of application sales. Competing accounting publishers can use the same published platform interfaces.
Five partners begin preparation in January 1981 for a January 1982 coordinated launch.

They retain their brands and may build mainboards, contract manufacture or buy Logix boards; buy custom chips from AION or qualified SGS; source qualified RAM freely; design local chassis/keyboards; and buy conforming monitors from Logix or others.
Anything outside an initial range may be supplied by Logix or third parties, with clear warranty and integration ownership.
No partner must manufacture a complete catalogue.

AION Software delivers and maintains German, French and Spanish CP/M/TUI, AIONix, Business Tools, Abacus and programming environments, coordinating underlying OS rights and release approval with independent DRI.
Use common APIs, document formats and shared cores with local resources.
Validate keyboards, accents, fonts, printing, sorting, numbers, currency and dates.

Clone manufacturers separately license other publishers including WordStar, dBASE and SSG General Ledger; local accounting requirements and language editions require separate publisher approval and qualification.
UK English editions and support serve Aion Tech.
Localisation is not a national software fork.
These agreements, preparations and January 1982 launches are accepted narrative additions.
Existing ecosystem projections already include North Star and Vector; replace their unsigned-prospect assumptions in the next numerical reassessment, never add their sales twice.
Germany, France, Spain and Aion Tech require country forecasts.
No automatic sales multiplier is awarded for the launch.

Transfer funding, localisation, pilot lots, marketing, Academy staffing, working capital and chip capacity must be costed before a revised investment/ROI claim; Reconcile 1981–1983 numerical planning with the current country, manufacturer and capacity assumptions; provisional transfer prices and capacity allowances are not signed contract terms.
Aion Tech ownership and consolidation remain open.
SGS receives a non-exclusive independent manufacture-and-sale licence for ERAv1 and all agreed custom controllers, including MMU, system, bus, storage, network and video controllers.
Each part and speed grade qualifies separately.
ERAv1 stays on 3 µm; no shrink is implied.
Preserve existing SMC rights.
AION provides launch supply for parts not yet qualified at SGS, so January clone delivery does not depend on simultaneous qualification of the entire portfolio.
Adam commits to supplying the staffing, equipment, licences and integration resources required by the agreed delivery plan.
No arbitrary dollar ceiling or fabricated cost estimate; procurement and staffing are reviewed against the November objective.
Non-exclusive funded development.
Autodesk retains its software ownership and cross-platform business; clear the underlying Interact contribution/porting rights with the founders, including Mike Riddle.
Logix supplies distribution and joint marketing, without a source buyout or forced platform exclusivity.
Professional 17-inch/800x600 hardware becomes available around June, not January.
Sponsorship is incremental project work, not counted as retail Team Edition sales.
Numerical planning must distinguish sponsorship provision from conditional CAD demand.
This is not a contractual funding ceiling, supplier quotation or confirmed shipment count.

All ERA² architectural numbers are engineering targets, with 16 MHz a stretch bin.
AION Labs alone manufactures ERA² initially; SGS-ATES excluded for at least 12–18 months after initial commercial availability.
Development dates are provisional; cost and financial forecasts remain unchanged.

Source portability is a separate commitment, not a substitute for the binary execution path.

The NCC 1979 programme publishes optional versioned extensions separate from the CP/M core; neither FlexiBUS nor Logix video is mandatory for all CP/M applications.
Fund CP/M maintenance alongside the next-generation programme; detailed duration and budget remain open.
Qualify named host/ISA/TPA/application editions and file interchange; no universal Aurelia binary or disk compatibility is promised.

eligibility: Any manufacturer or independent integrator may implement the published environment without a bespoke partnership or mandatory certification.
binary: Existing Z80 binaries require compatible instruction execution and the specified OS/runtime and memory behaviour; CP/M alone is insufficient.
Other processors need an appropriate port or execution solution.
hardware: Native video, keyboards, disks and printers may be exposed through adapters.
FlexiBUS and Logix video hardware are separate optional profiles.
Full hardware clones may implement those published interfaces under their applicable terms.
applications: Named supported platforms are tested configurations, not an exclusive permission list.
Independently implemented environments may run properly licensed applications; certification identifies precisely what AION tested.
scope: Released 8-bit Aurelia interfaces only.

licensing: Specification and self-test requirements are freely accessible.
Kit fee covers media, manuals and updates supplied with the kit.
Reference runtime adapters may be modified and redistributed without per-machine royalty under standard terms.
No automatic licence to redistribute CP/M, application binaries, firmware or trademarks; obtain each required licence separately.
Proprietary application source is not included.
delivery: Printed manuals/source listings and disks; host/media conversion quoted separately.
certification: Optional, configuration- and version-specific.
Manufacturer-declared compatibility is distinct from AION-tested application compatibility.
FlexiBUS electrical/protocol and Logix display tests are separate claims.

assumption.topic: Aurelia memory supply and protected Cambridge capacity, 1975–June 1978
statements: Fund the early fab, staffing, tools, working capital and qualification from Adam’s capital. Early ROM and SRAM sales provide customer feedback and operating revenue; they do not determine the pace of capital investment.

Plan for 10,000 Aurelias per month at the June 1978 launch, with an expansion scenario of 20,000. These are manufacturing planning cases, not recorded sales. Each computer consumes 32 16 Kbit DRAMs and two 4 Kbit SRAMs.

Use 30% attachment of the eight-chip 16 KiB RAM card as a provisioning scenario, without assigning its unresolved first commercial offering date. Reserve 100,000 accepted DRAMs and 10,000 accepted 4 Kbit SRAMs per month for external customers; these are planning allocations, not signed orders or guaranteed income.

Apply the existing finance premise once: forecast demand plus 5% good-output capacity. The 10,000-computer case therefore requires 466,200 DRAMs and 31,500 4 Kbit SRAMs per month. The 20,000-computer case requires 827,400 and 52,500 respectively. Do not add the earlier illustrative 10% allowance.

Before launch, fund and build one month of internal memory demand: 344,000 accepted DRAMs and 20,000 accepted 4 Kbit SRAMs, segregated from external orders. Replenish against consumption and revised demand; headroom does not imply permanent accumulation of unsold stock.

Provision 8,000 total wafer starts per month by December 1977: up to 6,000 DRAM, 500 4 Kbit SRAM, 500 ROM/1 Kbit SRAM, 500 released logic and 500 engineering starts. All allocations share one factory and its back-end capacity. Unused allocations may move only after route and load checks.

Require the March 1978 acceptance to demonstrate at least 575,000 accepted DRAMs and 31,500 accepted 4 Kbit SRAMs per month, or equivalent demonstrated spare capacity against actual shipments. Capacity demonstrations must cover the full route and shipped grade; forecasts are not measured results.

The 20,000-computer scenario requires expansion of DRAM, SRAM, assembly and test capacity. An option for up to 12,000 DRAM starts per month is an expansion objective, not installed capacity; no such capacity is credited to the initial line.

Recruit experienced process integration, DRAM, reliability, production test and maintenance staff early. Legitimate recruitment from established semiconductor manufacturers does not convey their trade secrets or process licences.

From May 1978, larger-memory and later processor research must stay inside the reserved engineering allocation or separately commissioned capacity; it must not consume committed Aurelia or external memory output.
